content: Stomatin, also referred to as human erythrocyte integral membrane protein band 7, is a protein encoded by the STOM gene in humans. Clinical Significance Stomatin is a 31 kDa integral membrane protein, named after the rare hereditary hemolytic anemia known as hereditary stomatocytosis. This protein is a member of a highly conserved family of integral membrane proteins. It is localized to the cell membrane of red blood cells and other cell types, where it is thought to regulate ion channels and transporters. A loss of proper localization of stomatin is associated with hereditary stomatocytosis, a specific form of hemolytic anemia. Function The STOM gene encodes a protein that belongs to a highly conserved family of integral membrane proteins. The encoded protein is found in the cell membrane of red blood cells and other cell types, where it may play a role in regulating ion channels and transporters. Disruption in the localization of this protein is linked to hereditary stomatocytosis, a type of hemolytic anemia. Although stomatin is widely distributed and constitutively expressed, suggesting it plays a critical role in cellular biology—potentially as a housekeeping component—its precise function remains unclear. The abundant presence of stomatin in membrane-protruding folds and extensions indicates it may have a structural role in the formation of these membrane structures and/or their anchorage to the actin cytoskeleton.
